source: Sweller and Cooper (1985) The use of worked examples as a substitute for problem solving in learning algebra, Exps 2-3
finding: Year 9 students who studied worked examples spent far less time on the learning phase than students who solved the same problems. Test-phase advantage was small in Exp 2 and clear in Exp 3.
numbers: Exp 2: N=20 (10 per group). First presentation, mean seconds per problem: worked 27.5 vs conventional 73.3. Test seconds 105.4 vs 127.1, not significant (U(10,10)=47). Test errors per problem 0.13 vs 0.50, p=.10. Exp 3: N=22 (11 per group), 4 problem types. First presentation 32.0 s vs 185.5 s (ratio 5.8). Test 43.6 s vs 78.1 s, U(11,11)=27.5, significant. Test errors 0.18 vs 1.64. Tests are Mann-Whitney, not parametric.
quote: worked examples require considerably less time to process than conventional problems
limits: Tiny cells. Same-school Year 9 algebra (change the subject of an equation). Exp 2 had a ceiling effect and the authors say the predicted test benefit was not found there. Experiment 1 of the paper is a memory study on equation recall (Year 9, Year 11, university), not a worked-example test.
agent_relevance: The robust part is efficiency: studying a solved case costs a fraction of solving. For an agent, the matching measure is tokens or steps spent, not only accuracy. Report both.

source: Sweller and Cooper (1985), Exps 4-5 (similar versus dissimilar test problems)
finding: The advantage held for test problems with the same structure as the examples and vanished for problems with new structure that used the same algebra. Putting dissimilar problems in between removed the advantage on the similar ones too.
numbers: Exp 4: N=40 (four groups of 10, order of similar and dissimilar test sets crossed). Similar problems tested first: worked group 48.5 s vs conventional 207.6 s per problem (U(10,10)=27, significant). Dissimilar: 62.6 vs 59.8 s (U=41, not significant). Errors on similar problems: worked group none (dash in table) vs 0.94; dissimilar 0.20 vs 0.20. When dissimilar problems came first, no group difference on either set (U=40 and U=38). Exp 5: N=24, time on acquisition matched. Worked group processed a mean 24.92 problems vs 8. Similar test 52.4 s vs 101.1 s (T(12)=8, significant), errors 0.13 vs 0.58. Dissimilar 163.7 vs 183.3 s, not significant; errors 1.06 vs 0.88.
quote: the results strongly confirm the specificity of schemas used in knowledge-based problem solving
limits: The paper's own reading: schemas were specific and easily forgotten. No far-transfer benefit at all in this paper. Small N, nonparametric tests, one domain. The earlier K23 text said the effect 'failed in geometry and kinematics'; that is not in this paper. Table layout was garbled in text extraction, so the error cells are read with some care.
agent_relevance: A stored solved case should be matched on structure, not just topic. Expect no gain on new-structure items. Do not claim a stored solution teaches a general skill. This is the strongest primary reason to retrieve by structure and test on both near and far items.

source: Cooper and Sweller (1987) Effects of schema acquisition and rule automation on mathematical problem-solving transfer, J Educ Psychol 79:347-362
finding: Four experiments (three algebra transformation, one algebra word problems). Students with heavy worked-example training or longer acquisition solved both similar and transfer problems better than students given conventional problems.
numbers: Not retrieved. Only the abstract wording was seen through search; no N, means or effect sizes.
limits: Full text paywalled. A 2000 commentary says the link from automated rules to transfer is only indirectly supported. The abstract claims transfer gains, which differs from the no-far-transfer pattern in the 1985 paper (d02). The difference, if real, may come from longer practice and rule automation.
agent_relevance: Do not cite a transfer size for this paper. Gap 1 stays open for the 1987 numbers.

source: Paas (1992) Training strategies for attaining transfer of problem-solving skill in statistics, J Educ Psychol 84:429-434
finding: Three computer-based training conditions: conventional problems, worked-out problems, completion (partly worked) problems. Worked and completion strategies gave better transfer than conventional; worked was best. The predicted lower time and effort during training was not found.
numbers: Not retrieved (abstract only, via search). No N or means.
limits: Full text not reachable (record shows no PDF). Per the abstract the full worked arm was the best, so 'completion as good as full' is not clearly supported here.
agent_relevance: Completion problems are not shown to beat full examples here; the best arm was the full worked one. Treat K13 as contested.

source: Nievelstein, van Gog, van Dijck and Boshuizen (2013) The worked example and expertise reversal effect in less structured tasks: learning to reason about legal cases, Contemp Educ Psychol 38:118-125
finding: With novice and advanced law students, worked examples beat problem solving for both groups. No expertise reversal appeared. Arms were process steps, worked examples, examples plus steps, and no support.
numbers: Abstract only: no N or effect sizes seen. Four conditions, two expertise levels.
quote: worked examples were more effective for learning than problem-solving
limits: Only the repository abstract was read; full text sits behind a login. Advanced students were still not experts. Authors expected examples to stay useful longer because the task takes long to master.
agent_relevance: Supports (weakly) keeping examples for ill-structured tasks, and suggests the reversal point comes later when the skill is hard. Needs numbers before it is used to set a gate.

source: Chen, Kalyuga and Sweller (2015) The worked example effect, the generation effect, and element interactivity, J Educ Psychol 107:689-704
finding: Novices: worked example effect for high element interactivity (solving geometry problems), generation effect (practice beats study) for low element interactivity (geometry formulae). With more expert learners the pattern became a generation effect for all materials.
numbers: No means, F values or N retrieved. Only abstract-level claims from search and the ERIC record.
limits: Secondary reading only. The 2018 review by Chen, Castro-Alonso, Paas and Sweller (d07) restates these results qualitatively and gives no statistics either.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open on size. The direction is clear: for simple items the stored example is not needed or is harmful. A cheap classifier for element interactivity is still untested.

source: Chen, Castro-Alonso, Paas and Sweller (2018) Undesirable difficulty effects in the learning of high-element interactivity materials, Front Psychol 9:1483
finding: Narrative review. Study-versus-practice effects flip with element interactivity: testing or generation helps for low interactivity, reverse or no effect for high interactivity. Chen 2015 novices fit this.
numbers: No worked-example statistics. Only imported effect sizes from other meta-analyses: testing effect 0.50 (Rowland 2014) and 0.56 (Schwieren 2017); generation effect 0.40 (Bertsch 2007). Examples listed: Leahy 2015 reverse testing effect with primary students; Hanham 2017 testing effect at low interactivity and none or reverse at high.
limits: Read through a fetch summarizer, so wording is not verbatim. Review, not data. Effect sizes quoted are for testing and generation, not for worked examples.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule of thumb for gating: show a solved case only where the item has many interacting steps; at low interactivity let the agent try first.

source: Tetzlaff, Simonsmeier, Peters and Brod (2025) A cornerstone of adaptivity: a meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect, Learn Instr 98
finding: Across studies, high instructional assistance helped learners with low prior knowledge and hurt learners with high prior knowledge. Effect is called robust across contexts.
numbers: 176 effect sizes, 60 experimental studies, 5,924 participants. Low prior knowledge: d=0.505 for high assistance. High prior knowledge: d=-0.428 (low assistance better). No worked-example-specific split seen.
limits: Seen only in search snippets and secondary summaries; the publisher page returned 403. Assistance covers many formats, not only worked examples. Moderator results not read.
agent_relevance: This is the first pooled size for the reversal: about half an SD each way. A gate on agent skill is worth testing, and the cross-over, not the average, is the thing to measure. K02 now has a meta-analytic anchor.

source: SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks (arXiv 2602.12670)
finding: Curated skill documents raise agent pass rates on average, for every one of seven model-harness setups. Self-generated skills do not. Gains do not shrink for stronger models.
numbers: 84 tasks, 11 domains, 7,308 trajectories, 5 runs per task. Mean pass: no skills 24.3, curated 40.6, self-generated 21.0. Examples: Opus 4.5 22.0 to 45.3 (self-gen 21.6); Haiku 4.5 11.0 to 27.7 (self-gen 11.0); Gemini 3 Flash 31.3 to 48.7. 16 of 84 tasks had negative skill deltas (worst -39.3 pp). By skill count: 1 skill +17.8 pp, 2-3 skills +18.6, 4+ skills +5.9. By length: detailed +18.8, compact +17.1, standard +10.1, comprehensive -2.9.
limits: Read through a fetch summarizer; table alignment is its best reading. Paper is inconsistent: 84 vs 86 tasks, and text says self-gen -1.3 pp while table means imply -3.3. Skills are expert-written procedures, not solved cases. Authors say gains may partly be more context. No worked-example ablation here.
agent_relevance: Strong case that a verified, curated library helps and a model-written one does not by itself. Fits the verify-before-store guardrail. No sign of reversal for stronger models in this range (Opus 4.5 gained more than Haiku).

source: Xu and Wu (2026) Skill availability and presentation granularity in LLM agents: a controlled SkillsBench study (arXiv 2605.31408)
finding: Having a skill document matters; how abstract it is, or whether it holds one worked example, changes little. This is the closest controlled test of entry form in an agent.
numbers: 30 oracle-validated tasks, 5 trials per cell, GPT-5.5 and DeepSeek V4-Flash, 1,800 runs. No skill: 31.3 percent and 26.0 percent. Skill conditions: +26.7 to +36.0 pp (GPT-5.5), +18.0 to +26.0 pp (DeepSeek). Low versus high abstraction: +0.7 pp [-10.0, +12.0] and -6.7 pp [-14.7, +0.7]. Adding one worked example to medium guidance: +0.7 pp [-5.3, +6.0] and +1.3 pp [-6.0, +9.3]. Rewritten variants 5.3 to 9.3 pp below the original curated skills for GPT-5.5.
limits: One benchmark subset, two models not compute-matched, wide intervals (power only for large effects). Skills are long documents, not short retrieved cases.
agent_relevance: Example inclusion and abstraction level are second-order effects at this size. Do not spend design effort on entry form before relevance and correctness are fixed. Gap 3 is narrowed but not closed: no full-solution versus skeleton arm at equal tokens.

source: Singh et al. (2026) ThinkRetrieve: retrieval-augmented reasoning traces for test-time scaling (arXiv 2608.10928)
finding: Retrieving a similar solved problem and inserting it inside the thinking trace at each step helps small reasoning models. Giving the same kind of examples once at the start (static in-context) does about nothing. Random retrieval gives part of the gain. Gains shrink as the model gets stronger.
numbers: AIME 2025 (30 problems, 3 seeds), columns standard thinking / sequential TTS / static ICL k=3 / random per-step / ThinkRetrieve: R1-Qwen-1.5B 14.4/23.3/16.7/25.6/30.0; Qwen3-1.7B 24.4/22.2/23.3/27.8/35.6; Qwen3.5-2B 17.8/31.1/20.0/28.9/34.4; Qwen3-4B 63.3/64.4/62.2/65.6/66.7; Qwen3-8B 67.8/68.9/66.7/66.7/71.1. MATH-500 Qwen3-8B 93.2/94.0/92.9/93.5/94.8. Max gain over TTS +13.4 points (Qwen3-1.7B). Example bank NuminaMath. One ThinkRetrieve pass beat self-consistency at matched 8K budget on a MATH-500 subset.
quote: per-step in-trace injection is necessary (S-ICL underperforms) and semantic retrieval relevance is necessary (Rand underperforms)
limits: Models are 1.5B to 8B only. AIME has 30 items so one item is 3.3 points. Injected tokens count against budget but are not generated; authors claim fewer generated tokens (12,913 vs 15,847). Authors' own limit: depends on corpus coverage. Possible leakage audited post hoc (Table 4).
agent_relevance: Where a retrieved case helps, it helps by arriving at the point of need and by matching structure. Static prefix examples (here are three solved cases) are the weak form. Relevant to S-state hooks: fetch after a stall, not before the first try.

source: Chen, Bai and Yuille (2026) The Compliance Trap: diagnosing how AI agents consume conflicting memory (arXiv 2607.10608)
finding: On WebArena, plain retrieval of online-generated memory gave no reliable gain, whether gated by relevance or not. When stored memory conflicts with the task, agents adopt it at the first decision point, and damage grows with the model's baseline skill.
numbers: Table 1, 684 non-map WebArena tasks: unconditional retrieval Qwen3.5-9B -1.9 pp, 27B +1.7 pp; relevance-gated -2.3 and -1.7 pp. Persistent conflicting memory on 77 tasks: hurts every model, up to -20.8 pp (Qwen3.5-27B) and -14.9 pp (Gemini-3-Flash); paired damage Qwen3.5-27B -25.5 pp vs Gemma-4-E4B -2.1 pp (baselines 49 and 23 percent). MemTrapBench, 231 tasks, persistent conflicting: Qwen3.5-9B -9.5, 27B -21.2, Gemma-4-26B -10.8, Gemini-3-Flash -26.0 pp. Persistent helpful memory: +25 to +31 pp. Cross-task control near zero.
quote: Stronger agents therefore suffer larger absolute damage because each compliance event erases more baseline capability.
limits: Conflicting and helpful memories are hand-built in MemTrapBench, so the +25 to +31 is a designed positive control. WebArena subset of 77 tasks gives wide intervals. Gemma and Qwen families plus Gemini-3-Flash. Compliance rate is about equal across models; damage differs because the starting point differs.
agent_relevance: A library entry is high-stakes: a wrong or mismatched case is followed at the first step and the agent rarely recovers. Gating must be on correctness and match, not on relevance score alone. Good test: inject conflicting entries and measure recovery.

source: How memory management impacts LLM agents: an empirical study of experience-following behavior (arXiv 2505.16067, ACL 2026)
finding: Adding every executed experience to memory makes the agent worse than a small fixed memory. Adding only evaluator-approved experiences makes it better. Agents copy the output of the most similar stored record, so errors propagate.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini. Fixed memory vs add-all vs strict-evaluator (success or accuracy): RegAgent 67.53 / 55.48 / 70.95; EHRAgent 16.75 / 13.05 / 38.50; AgentDriver 40.11 / 32.32 / 51.00; CIC-IoT 71.50 / 59.90 / 85.40. Add-all minus fixed: -12.05, -3.70, -7.79, -11.60 points. Coarse evaluators fall between (e.g. EHRAgent coarse C1 26.19, C3 34.66). History-based deletion on top of strict: EHRAgent 38.67 to 42.06, CIC-IoT 85.40 to 89.60 with smaller memories. Input-output similarity correlation about r=1 on RegAgent.
limits: Read through a fetch summarizer. Only GPT-4o-mini in main tables. Bad-record share is not reported, so there is still no slope of accuracy against percent wrong. Tasks are regression, EHR coding, driving and traffic classification, not reasoning problems.
agent_relevance: Closest measured answer to gap 8. A strict verifier before storing is worth 4 to 22 points over an open door in these four tasks, and add-all loses 4 to 12 points against doing nothing. Still missing: a dose-response by wrong share.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025/2026) Dynamic Cheatsheet: test-time learning with adaptive memory (arXiv 2504.07952, EACL 2026)
finding: A curated, rewritten cheatsheet lifts Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o on hard math, far more than appending the full history of past questions and answers. It does little for reasoning-tuned models, small models, or when retrieved items are poor.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet: AIME 2024 baseline 23.3, DC-Cu 50.0, DC-RS 46.7; AIME 2025 6.7 to 36.7; GPQA-Diamond 59.6 to 61.1 (DC-RS 68.7). Full-history appending (AIME only): Claude 26.7 and 6.7; GPT-4o 13.3 and 3.3 (baselines 20.0 and 6.7). GPT-4o Game of 24: 10.0 to 93.0 (DC-Cu), 99.0 (DC-RS), by storing code. GPT-4o GPQA 57.1 unchanged; MMLU-Pro Engineering 53.2 to 44.0 (DC-Cu). GPT-4o-mini AIME 2024: both DC variants below baseline. DeepSeek R1 and o1: minimal or inconsistent gains.
limits: Read through a fetch summarizer. AIME sets are 30 problems per year, so 3.3-point steps. Test questions arrive in sequence and memory is built on the same stream, so part of the gain is online learning on near-duplicate problem types. Full-history appending is unfiltered and grows in length; it is not a retrieved raw case.
agent_relevance: Head-to-head of raw history against distilled notes, with distilled winning by 23 points (Claude AIME24) and raw hurting GPT-4o. Contradicts SkillEvolBench (d15), where retrieved raw trajectories beat distilled skills. Different raw form (all history vs retrieved same-family) probably explains it. Also shows that memory helps mid-strength models and not weak or reasoning-tuned ones.

source: Lei et al. (2026) SkillEvolBench: benchmarking the evolution from episodic experience to procedural skills (arXiv 2605.24117)
finding: Distilled skill libraries often did worse on frozen deployment tasks than retrieving the raw compacted trajectories, and static curated skills hurt most models. Writing more skills or bigger libraries did not fix it.
numbers: 180 tasks, six environments, ten model configurations, three harnesses. Raw-Trajectory baseline is strongest by mean: RSR 48.2, ESR 37.6, ARSR 44.7, CompSR 25.7 percent. Curated-Static vs No-Skill: improves 2 models, ties 1, hurts 7, mean ESR change -2.44 pp. Gemini 3 Flash ESR 35.6 (no skill) to 27.8 with the largest self-generated library; Claude Sonnet 4.5 35.6 to 30.0. Opus 4.6 self-generated: +5.5 pp local (LSR) and +10.0 pp (RSR) but lower ESR, CSSR and CompSR.
quote: Raw-trajectory reuse frequently outperforms distilled skills
limits: Deployment tests are built to catch shortcuts, shifts and composition, so they are hard. Raw-Trajectory retrieves same-family traces, which is a generous control. Percent success on 180 tasks with few per cell. Skills here are written by a model from compacted trajectories.
agent_relevance: Do not assume abstraction beats the concrete case. The abstraction step loses cues. Pair the skeleton with the raw case, and test the skeleton against the case at equal tokens. Raises doubts about K17 (distilled library gains) as a general rule.

source: LLM Shepherding: pay for hints, not answers (arXiv 2601.22132)
finding: A small model that gets the first part of a large model's answer as a prefix does better the more of the solution it is given. This is a partial-solution (completion) scaffold, with a monotone curve on GSM8K and a bumpy one on code.
numbers: GSM8K, SLM Llama-3.2-3B with hints from Llama-3.3-70B: hint size 0, 10, 30, 50, 70, 90 percent gives 77.5, 81.1, 81.7, 85.4, 89.8, 94.1 percent. LLM alone 98.0; SLM alone 73.0 in another table. HumanEval accuracy dips at 10, 30 and 60 percent and peaks at 90 percent (75.6). Cost reduction at default: 65.4 percent on GSM8K for 89.1 percent accuracy.
limits: Read through a fetch summarizer. One model pair for most results. The 0 percent value (77.5) and the SLM-alone value (73.0) differ without explanation. Prefix is the strong model's own start, not a hand-written faded example. Verifiable tasks only.
agent_relevance: For a weaker model, more of the solution is better, so fading (removing late steps) should be tested on the weak side only, if at all. Nothing here tests backward fading as a teaching device. Gap 6 stays open for fading proper; this gives the partial-prefix dose curve.

source: Give me a hint: can LLMs take a hint to solve math problems? (arXiv 2410.05915)
finding: A correct hint helps most instruct and closed models a little. A wrong hint or a hint from another problem hurts by about 7 points on average. Base models are hurt even by a correct hint.
numbers: 700 MATH problems (100 per topic, 20 per level), 11 models. Mean accuracy: no hint 0.5355, correct hint 0.5615, adversarial 0.4674, random 0.4628. Base models 0.5385 to 0.5104 with correct hint; random hint 0.2871. Instruct 0.5471 to 0.5601; math-tuned 0.6180 to 0.6485; closed 0.6685 to 0.7186. Gemini-1.5-Flash 0.6114 to 0.6686. Llama-3.1-8B base 0.5571 to 0.5143.
limits: Read through a fetch summarizer; authors' Table 4 has duplicated rows. Models from 2024; hints are text hints, not solved cases. Single run per cell on 700 problems.
agent_relevance: A wrong stored hint costs about 2.5 times what a right one gains (-6.8 vs +2.6 points). So the threshold for storing should favour precision. Supports K18.

source: Xiao et al. (2025) The role of diversity in in-context learning for large language models (arXiv 2505.19426)
finding: Picking examples for similarity alone is best on easy tasks. Mixing similarity with diversity is better on harder tasks and under distribution shift. On GSM8K at four shots nothing separates the methods.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B, K=4. GSM8K: random 66.90, TopK 65.30, diversity 66.92, TopK-Div 66.12. SST-2: TopK 94.13 vs TopK-Div 92.75. GeoQuery: TopK 62.79, Div 33.79, TopK-Div 71.14 (about +8 over TopK; other models +9 to +11). Gain from diversity on GeoQuery: 5.11 points on easy items, 10.72 on hard. SQuAD: TopK-Div trails by 0.87 on easy, leads by 2.23 on hard. Zero-shot to 4-shot on SQuAD: 42.30 to 73-76.
limits: 7B to 9B open models (70B in ablation). Tasks are mostly not reasoning. Read through a fetch summarizer. Contrast in the human sense (matched pair differing in one feature) is not tested; diversity is coverage by embedding.
agent_relevance: Weak support for: difference between examples matters on hard items, retrieval match on easy ones. Does not decide gap 5 for reasoning. A test with matched contrast pairs versus two near-duplicates at equal tokens is still needed.

source: When successful memories mislead embodied agents: memory adaptation for task-conditioned execution (MATE) (arXiv 2609.35808)
finding: Raw successful trajectories contain actions that do not fit the new task. Converting a retrieved trajectory into condition-action-effect steps, normalising actions and picking a representation within a fixed budget restores its use.
numbers: 134 ALFWorld tasks: 81.3 percent (Qwen2.5-14B) and 93.3 percent (Qwen2.5-72B) with MATE, at about one-tenth the tokens of raw trajectories. Authors say verified action normalisation is the main mechanism.
limits: Abstract only (arXiv abstract page); baselines for raw trajectories not seen. Embodied household tasks, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: Another point for editing the retrieved case before use, at a fraction of the tokens. It argues that entry form matters, which d10 did not find for documents. Reconcile by task type: action-like tasks versus reasoning.

source: Lekshmi-Narayanan et al. (2026) Self-explanation tutor for active study of CS1 worked examples (arXiv 2608.25180)
finding: An LLM judge can mark student self-explanations of code lines well enough to power a tutor. Students revised rather than quit and explanations grew more complete.
numbers: Judge vs human expert: precision .95, recall .87, F1 .91, accuracy 83.8 percent. Deployment: 8 students, 409 attempts; completeness gain across attempts Wilcoxon p<.001; only 3 of 8 students did a pre-test.
limits: Pilot with N=8, no control group, no learning outcome versus a control. It tests the tutor, not the self-explanation effect.
agent_relevance: A model can check a self-explanation step cheaply, so the self-explanation operator can be audited. It says nothing about whether self-explanation helps the explainer at a given strength (gap 7 stays open).
